title: Why text isn't searchable: strings to numbers
summary: Exact matching fails because people use different words for the same thing. The fix is to turn every chunk into a vector so similarity becomes arithmetic, which turns retrieval into a sparse storage problem with two very different layouts.
html:
You have chunks now. Day 2 ended with five stages and a write path that produces something a read path can search. Today is about the gap between those two sentences, because "search the chunks" is doing a lot of quiet work. A chunk is a string. Strings are not searchable in the way retrieval needs, and understanding exactly why is what makes everything from Day 4 onward make sense.

What grep actually gives you

Start with what you already have. You can grep a corpus. That gives you exact substring matching, which answers one question well: does this literal sequence of bytes appear in this document. For retrieval that question is almost never the one you want answered.

Suppose the chunk says "the queen is the only fertile female in the colony" and the user asks "who lays the eggs?" There is no shared substring worth anything. Grep returns nothing. The chunk is the correct answer and your search returned empty.

Run it the other way and it fails differently. Search for "colony" across a corpus about beekeeping and you get four hundred hits with no ordering. Grep has no notion of more relevant, only present. It gives you a set, and retrieval needs a ranked list.

So you need two things grep cannot express: a similarity that survives different wording, and a score you can sort by.

The vocabulary problem

The wording issue is worse than it looks. There is a well-known result from Furnas and colleagues in 1987, studying how people name things: two people asked to pick a keyword for the same familiar object choose the same word less than twenty percent of the time. Not for obscure things. For ordinary ones.

You have seen this in your own systems. The thing the docs call a volume, the runbook calls a LUN, the support ticket calls the disk, and the alert calls it a backing store. All four refer to the same object. A literal matcher treats them as four unrelated tokens.

This is the single fact that motivates everything else in this course. If people reliably used the same words, retrieval would be a solved problem and we would all still be running grep.

The move: text becomes a point

Here is the leap. Instead of comparing strings to strings, turn every chunk into a vector, a list of numbers, and compare the numbers.

The simplest version. Collect every distinct word in your corpus into a vocabulary, say fifty thousand of them, and fix an order. Now any chunk becomes a vector of length fifty thousand, where position i holds the count of vocabulary word i in that chunk. "the queen lays eggs" becomes a vector that is zero everywhere except at four positions.

vocabulary:  [ ..., colony, eggs, lays, queen, the, ... ]
"the queen lays eggs"
             [ ..., 0,      1,    1,    1,     1,   ... ]

This is called bag of words, and the name is the honest part. You have thrown away word order entirely. "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce identical vectors. That is a real loss and you should not pretend otherwise. Recovering order is exactly what the transformer encoder buys you on Day 9. For now the loss is worth it, because of what you get in exchange.

What the geometry buys you

Once chunks are points in a space, similarity becomes arithmetic. Two chunks that use overlapping words sit near each other. Two that share nothing sit far apart. "Find relevant text" becomes "find nearby points", and nearby is something a computer can compute and, more importantly, something it can rank.

That solves the second of our two problems immediately. You get a score, so you get an ordering. The first problem, different words for the same thing, is not solved yet. Bag of words still treats volume and LUN as unrelated dimensions. Keep that open. It stays open until Day 9.

What you have gained is the right shape of problem. Retrieval is now nearest neighbour search in a vector space, and that is a problem with fifty years of literature behind it.

Sparsity, and why this is a storage problem

Now the part that should feel familiar. Take a 100 word chunk against a 50,000 word vocabulary. After removing repeats you have maybe 70 distinct words. So the vector has 70 nonzero entries out of 50,000. That is 99.86 percent zeros.

Stored naively as float32, one chunk costs 50,000 times 4 bytes, so 200 KB, to hold about 280 bytes of actual information. A million chunks would be 200 GB of almost entirely zeros. Nobody does this.

You store it sparse, as pairs of index and value, and now you are making the same decisions you would make for any sparse matrix. That is the honest framing: the first real retrieval data structure is a compressed sparse representation, and the choice of representation determines what queries are cheap.

There are two ways to lay it out, and this is a genuine fork in the road, not a detail.

Row major, by documentColumn major, by term
You storefor each chunk, its list of (term, count)for each term, its list of (chunk, count)
Cheap questionwhat is in this chunkwhich chunks contain this term
Known asa document vectoran inverted index
Leads tovector search, Days 15 to 30BM25 and lexical search, Day 31

The inverted index is the older idea and it is not obsolete. It is what every search engine you have ever used runs on, and on Day 31 you will meet BM25, which is still hard to beat. The reason this course spends Days 15 to 30 on the vector side instead is that vectors generalise to the dense embeddings of Day 9, where the vocabulary mismatch problem finally gets solved. On Day 33 you will put both back together, because production systems run them side by side.

Why raw counts are the wrong numbers

One last problem before tomorrow. Use raw counts and the vector is dominated by whichever words are most frequent, which means the, of, and, is. Every chunk in English has a large value at those positions. Every chunk therefore looks similar to every other chunk, and your similarity score is mostly measuring how much ordinary English each chunk contains.

The fix is not to delete common words, though stopword lists do exist and help a little. The fix is to weight each word by how much it actually distinguishes one chunk from another. A word appearing in every chunk tells you nothing. A word appearing in three chunks out of ten thousand tells you a great deal.

Turning that sentence into a formula is exactly tomorrow's lesson. Day 4 is TF-IDF from scratch, and by the end of it you will have a working scorer you wrote yourself.
exercise:
1. Measure your own sparsity. Take any text file you have lying around, a README, a log, a design doc. In Python: split it into 100 word chunks, build the vocabulary across all chunks, then print the vocabulary size, the average number of distinct words per chunk, and the resulting sparsity as a percentage. Ten lines of code. The number will be higher than you expect.

2. Find a vocabulary mismatch in your own world. Write down one object in a system you work on that has three or more names across documentation, code, and conversation. This is the concrete instance of the problem the next eight days are solving, and it is worth having a real one in your head rather than a bee example.

3. Predict a failure. Take the two sentences "the queen lays up to 1000 eggs per day" and "egg production peaks in spring". Build the bag of words vector for each by hand. How many dimensions overlap? Given that overlap, would a count based scorer rank these as related? Keep your answer, because on Day 9 you will run the same pair through a real embedding model and compare.
